prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing optical frequency standards to the 1e-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a clean, original invention with an unambiguous measurable outcome. The magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift on a lattice-trapped neutral-atom ensemble, which gives Lamb-Dicke confinement together with the signal-to-noise of many atoms. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 followed, and independent laboratories now reproduce them in intercomparisons. That is the kind of discovery-by-instrument I weigh most heavily in atomic physics: a new limit on what we can measure, and how accurately. It already supports tests of fundamental constants and of relativity, relativistic geodesy and the roadmap for redefining the second. The attribution is the most compact on the list: Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking the technique to extreme accuracy and stability and for the many-body clock work. Seven of the eight members place B007 in their top four, and the support is broad across subfields, which matters more to me than the number of first places.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit. Magic-wavelength lattice clocks were developed in parallel by several strong groups (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and Takamoto among others), and Ye's record accuracy builds on the optical-comb work already honoured in 2005 and on ion-clock work honoured in 2012, so the committee could read this as an incremental step on prior prizes. A second concern is that much of what makes the clock matter, the redefinition of the second and geodesy, is still prospective rather than realised. I judge that this weakens the case only mildly, because the accuracy and reproducibility results are already in hand. I also note that I am relying on recalled priority history rather than verified records, as I did in my opening ballot.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B005) first, as a clean theory-prediction plus experimental-discovery story that opened twistronics, and places optical lattice clocks second.
responses.response: I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 observations is an unusually clean sequence, and I keep B005 as my first alternative. I part from the proposal on two points. The experimental credit is genuinely unsettled: Jarillo-Herrero's group did the work, but Cao, the first author, is outside the credited names, and Dean, Young and Yazdani also have strong claims. And the field is still moving fast, so what the single most important result will turn out to be is less settled than for lattice clocks. The clocks have already been tested against each other at the 1e-18 level. I would also resist treating the 'new platform' argument as a stronger sign of maturity than a reproduced measurement standard.

responses.point: Pearce ranks lattice clocks first as a genuine instrument breakthrough, but flags the attribution problem for twisted bilayer graphene (the omission of Cao) and, as chair-level concern, the strain of crediting individuals in large collaborations such as IceCube.
responses.response: I share your reading of the clocks as an instrument breakthrough, and I accept your attribution worry about B005 as a real obstacle. I would qualify your relative comfort about the two-person lattice-clock pair. It is cleaner than the alternatives, but it is not free of contested priority, because Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and Takamoto also contributed. I would therefore want the citation worded around the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realisation at extreme accuracy rather than around the clock as a whole. That wording matches what Katori and Ye each did.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the anyon statistics case (B001) first as a deep conceptual result, with theory by Leinaas and Myrheim confirmed experimentally around 2020, and rates the optical lattice clocks fourth as clean and important but mainly a precision achievement.
responses.response: I take the point that anyonic statistics is conceptually deeper in the sense of changing what kinds of particles are allowed, and I do not equate measurement precision with that kind of depth. But the shortlisted B001 has six credited names and an experimental credit that you yourself describe as unresolved, and some interferometer interpretations remain debated. A clock is a counterweight on that axis: the result is a measured number reproduced by independent laboratories, with unambiguous authorship. I would be willing to see B001 treated as a future-year candidate once the experimental attribution settles. I do not think a lack of conceptual novelty counts against the clocks, since the magic-wavelength insight is itself a new idea.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks lattice clocks first, with the magic-angle graphene trio second, and calls the two-laureate Katori-Ye configuration coherent and defensible.
responses.response: I agree with the configuration. One thing I would flag for the later rounds is her suggestion of keeping to two laureates. I see no reason to add a third name: the temptation would be to bring in a comb or ion-clock contributor to give the prize a wider base, and that would blur an otherwise clear attribution to the lattice-clock idea. If a second part were wanted, I would rather pair the clocks with a distinct achievement than dilute the citation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to separate the theoretical magic-wavelength proposal from the first experimental strontium clock, and how to weigh Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and Takamoto, whom the credited pair omits.
How much weight overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-clock prize should carry against the lattice-clock invention.
Whether the experimental credit for twisted bilayer graphene (B005), in particular the first-author question, can be resolved well enough for it to compete as a joint or alternative prize.
My assessment of priority and recent clock-comparison results rests on recalled history, not verified records.
statement.conflict_note: Possible connections to flag from my profile: I spent part of my doctoral period in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall's optical-frequency-comb work is the background to the lattice-clock programme at JILA where Jun Ye works. I am not aware of any direct collaboration or co-authorship with Katori or Ye in the provided profile, so I do not think this requires recusal, but the committee should know. I am also a quantum-optics and quantum-memory researcher, a field adjacent to atom interferometry (B043), which is one of my alternatives. No other specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
